'''Pal Maliga ''' is a plant [[Molecule|molecular]] [[biologist]]. He is Distinguished Professor of Plant Biology and Laboratory [[Director (education)|Director]] at the [[Waksman Institute of Microbiology]], [[Rutgers University]]. He is known for developing the [[technology]] of [[chloroplast]] [[genome]] engineering in land plants and its applications in basic [[science]] and [[biotechnology]].
<!--
===Early life and education===

Pal Maliga was born in Budapest on February 23, 1946. He received an M.S. degree in Genetics and Microbiology from [[Eötvös Loránd University]], Budapest, in 1969 and a PhD from the József Attila University, Szeged, in 1972. 
Career
Between 1969 - 1982 Pal Maliga held appointments at the Biological Research Center (BRC), Hungarian Academy of Sciences, Szeged, in the Institute of Genetics (1969-1974) and the Institute of Plant Physiology (1974-1983) where his research group developed tobacco into the model system for organellar genetics in land plants. From 1973 to 1974, he spent a year in the Max Planck Institute for Biology in Tübingen, where he studied protoplast isolation and fusion in George Melchers’s laboratory. Between 1982 and 1983 he was a visiting scientist in the laboratory of Mary-Dell Chilton, Washington University, St Louis, MO, where he was exposed to Agrobacterium biology. He was Research Director of Advanced Genetic Sciences, Manhattan, KS (1983-1984) and Research Director for Plant Cellular Biology, Advanced Genetic Sciences, Inc., Oakland, CA (1984-1989). In 1989 he joined Rutgers University, where he currently holds appointments in the Department of Plant Biology, New Brunswick, NJ and the Waksman Institute of Microbiology, Piscataway, NJ.
-->

==Research==
=== Chloroplast genome engineering === 
The Maliga group in Szeged isolated chloroplast-encoded antibiotic-resistance<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Maliga, P, Sz-Breznovits, A, Marton, L | title = Streptomycin resistant plants from callus culture of haploid tobacco  | journal = Nature New Biology | volume =  244 | issue =  131| pages = 29–30 | date = July 1973 | pmid = 4515911 | doi = 10.1038/NEWBIO244029A0 | s2cid = 26838425}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Cseplo, A, Maliga, P  | title = Lincomycin resistance, a new type of maternally inherited mutation in Nicotiana plumbaginifolia  | journal = Current Genetics | volume =  6 | issue =  2| pages = 105–109 | date = November 1982 | pmid = 24186475 | doi = 10.1007/BF00435208 | s2cid = 7925902}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Cseplo, A, Maliga, P  | title = Large scale isolation of maternally inherited lincomycin resistance mutations in diploid Nicotiana plumbaginifolia protoplast cultures | journal = Molecular and General Genetics | volume =  196 | issue =  3| pages = 407–412 | date = 1984 | pmid = | doi = 10.1007/BF00436187 | s2cid = 24421287}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Svab Z, Maliga P | title = Mutation proximal to the tRNA binding region of the Nicotiana plastid 16S rRNA confers resistance to spectinomycin | journal = Molecular and General Genetics | volume =  228 | issue =  1–2| pages = 316–319 | date = August 1991 | pmid =  1832206 | doi = 10.1007/BF00282483 | s2cid = 34949950}}</ref> and herbicide-resistant [[mutant]]s<ref>
{{cite journal | vauthors = Cseplo, A, Medgyesy, P, Hideg, E, Demeter, S, Marton, L, Maliga, P | title = Triazine-resistant Nicotiana mutants from photomixotrophic cell cultures | journal = Molecular and General Genetics | volume =  200 | pages = 508–510 | date = August 1985 | issue = 3 | pmid =  | doi = 10.1007/BF00425742 | s2cid = 44212543}} 
</ref> in [[Cultured cell|cultured]] tobacco [[Cell (biology)|cells]] and have shown that chloroplast-encoded antibiotic-resistance gives a selective advantage to chloroplasts in cultured cells.<ref>
{{cite journal | vauthors = Moll, B, Polsby, L, Maliga, P | title = Streptomycin and lincomycin resistances are selective plastid markers in cultured Nicotiana cells | journal = Molecular and General Genetics | volume =  221 | pages = 245–250 | date = December 1989 | issue = 2 | pmid =  | doi = 10.1007/BF00261727 | s2cid = 19879921}}</ref> The ability to selectively enrich resistant chloroplasts was the foundation for obtaining chloroplast genome-engineered (transplastomic) tobacco plants.<ref>
{{cite journal | vauthors = Maliga, P | title = Plastid transformation in higher plants | journal =  Annual Review of Plant Biology | volume = 55 | pages = 289–313 | date = June 2004 | pmid =  15377222| doi = 10.1146/ANNUREV.ARPLANT.55.031903.141633 | s2cid = 36725756}}</ref> Extensive recombination of chloroplast [[genome]]s after chloroplast fusion confirmed homologous recombination in chloroplasts,<ref>
{{cite journal | vauthors = Medgyesy, P, Fejes, E, Maliga, P | title = Interspecific chloroplast recombination in a Nicotiana somatic hybrid | journal = Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America | volume = 82 | pages = 6960–6964 | date = October 1985 | issue = 20 | pmid =  16593619| doi = 10.1073/PNAS.82.20.6960 | pmc = 391289 | bibcode = 1985PNAS...82.6960M | s2cid = 20080861}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Fejes, E, Maliga, P | title = Extensive homologous chloroplast DNA recombination in the pt14 Nicotiana somatic hybrid | journal = Theoretical and Applied Genetics | volume = 79 | pages = 28–32 | date = 1990 | issue = 1 | pmid =  24226115| doi = 10.1007/BF00223782 | s2cid = 1575818}}</ref> providing a template for the design of chloroplast transformation vectors.
The Maliga laboratory achieved tobacco (Nicotiana tabacum) chloroplast genome transformation in 1990 by selection for spectinomycin resistance encoded in the 16S rRNA, a process that was made efficient  by selection for chimeric antibiotic resistance genes.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Svab, Z, Hajdukiewicz, P, Maliga, P | title = Stable transformation of plastids in higher plants | journal = Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America | volume = 87 | pages = 8526–8530 | date = 1990 | issue = 21 | pmid =  11607112| doi = 10.1073/PNAS.87.21.8526 | pmc = 54989 | bibcode = 1990PNAS...87.8526S | s2cid = 8024062}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Svab, Z, Maliga, P | title = High-frequency plastid transformation in tobacco by selection for a chimeric aadA gene | journal = Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America | volume = 90 | pages = 913–917 | date = February 1993 | issue = 3 | pmid =  8381537| doi = 10.1073/pnas.90.3.913 | pmc = 45780 | bibcode = 1993PNAS...90..913S | s2cid = 7281078| doi-access = free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Carrer, H, Hockenberry, TN, Svab, Z, Maliga, P | title = Kanamycin resistance as a selectable marker for plastid transformation in tobacco | journal = Molecular and General Genetics | volume = 241 | pages = 49–56 | date = October 2004 | issue = 1–2 | pmid =  8232211| doi = 10.1007/BF00280200 | s2cid = 2291268}}</ref> The significance of chloroplast genome engineering as a tool to improve photosynthetic efficiency was recognized early on.<ref>
{{cite news | vauthors =  | title = Step Seen Toward Altering Photosynthesis | work= New York Times | date = November 2, 1990 | pmid =  | doi = | s2cid = }}</ref>  In [[Arabidopsis thaliana|arabidopsis]] (Arabidopsis thaliana) efficient chloroplast transformation required knocking out a nuclear gene.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Yu, Q, Lutz, K, Maliga, P | title = Efficient plastid transformation in Arabidopsis | journal = Plant Physiology | volume = 175 | pages = 186–193 | date = 2017 | issue = 1 | pmid =  28739820| doi = 10.1104/pp.17.00857 | pmc = 5580780 | s2cid = 206339557}} 
</ref> The toolkit for chloroplast genome engineering was completed by post-transformation excision of marker genes using phage site-specific recombinases.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Lutz, K, Maliga, P | title = Construction of marker-free transplastomic plants | journal = Current Opinion in Biotechnology | date = 2007| volume = 18 | issue = 2 | pages = 107–114 | pmid =  17339108| doi = 10.1016/J.COPBIO.2007.02.003 | s2cid = 40899963}}</ref>

=== Agrobacterium transformation === 
The Maliga team constructed the pPZP Agrobacterium binary vector family,<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Hajdukiewicz P, Svab Z, Maliga P | title = The small, versatile pPZP family of Agrobacterium binary vectors for plant transformation | journal = Plant Molecular Biology | volume = 25 | pages = 989–994 | date = September 1994| issue = 6 | pmid =  7919218| doi = 10.1007/BF00014672 | s2cid = 9877624}}</ref> that served as the backbone for the CAMBIA and GATEWAY Agrobacterium vectors. Currently  they are engaged in reengineering Agrobacterium for DNA delivery to chloroplasts,<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Matsuoka, A, Maliga, P | title = Prospects for Reengineering Agrobacterium tumefaciens for T-DNA delivery to Chloroplasts | journal = Plant Physiology | volume = 186 | pages = 215–220 | date = 2021 | pmid =  33620481| doi = 10.1093/plphys/kiab081 | pmc = 8154051 | s2cid = 232017220}}</ref> so that chloroplast transformation can be achieved by the floral dip protocol.

=== Chloroplast transcription === 
Chloroplast reverse genetics revealed the distinct role of two plastid RNA polymerases.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Allison, LA, Simon, LD, Maliga, P | title = Deletion of rpoB reveals a second distinct transcription system in plastids of higher plants | journal = The EMBO Journal | date = 1996 | volume = 15 | issue = 11 | pages = 2802–2809 | pmid =  8654377| doi = 10.1002/j.1460-2075.1996.tb00640.x | pmc = 450217 | s2cid = 39505448}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Hajdukiewicz, P, Allison, LA, Maliga, P | title = The two RNA polymerases encoded by the nuclear and the plastid compartments transcribe distinct groups of genes in tobacco plastids | journal = The EMBO Journal | date = 1997 | volume = 16 | issue = 13 | pages = 4041–4048 | pmid =  9233813| doi = 10.1093/emboj/16.13.4041 | pmc = 1170027 | s2cid = 10769603}}</ref> The Maliga lab characterised plastid promoters in vivo and in vitro, and identified proteins that are parts of the plastid PEP transcription complex.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Suzuki, J, Ytterberg, AJ, Beardslee, TA, Allison, LA, vanWijk, KJ, Maliga, P | title = Affinity purification of the tobacco plastid RNA polymerase and in vitro reconstitution of the holoenzyme | journal = Plant J. | date = 2004 | volume = 40 | issue = 1 | pages = 164–172 | pmid =  15361150| doi = 10.1111/J.1365-313X.2004.02195.X | s2cid = 24662704| doi-access = free }}</ref>

===Expression of recombinant proteins in chloroplasts===
One of the first biotechnological applications of chloroplast engineering was expression of Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) crystal toxins genes, yielding 3-5% of the total leaf protein. Importantly, the insecticidal protein could be translated from the bacterial AU-rich mRNA, while for nuclear expression only synthetic GC-rich mRNAs could be used.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = McBride, KE, Svab, Z, Schaaf, DJ, Hogan, PS, Stalker, DM, Maliga, P | title = Amplification of a Chimeric Bacillus Gene in Chloroplasts Leads to an Extraordinary Level of an Insecticidal Protein in Tobacco | journal = Bio/Technology | date = 1995 | volume = 13 | issue = 4 | pages = 362–365 | pmid =  9634777| doi = 10.1038/NBT0495-362 | s2cid = 2154428}}</ref> Since then, the Maliga laboratory developed chloroplast expression tools that yield 25% tetanus subunit vaccine<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Tregoning, J, Nixon, P, Kuroda, H, Svab, Z, Clare, S, Bowe, F, Fairweather, N, Ytterberg, J, vanWijk, KJ, Dougan, G, Maliga, P | title = Expression of tetanus toxin fragment C in tobacco chloroplasts | journal = Nucleic Acids Res. | date = August 1985 | volume = 31 | issue = 4 | pages = 1174–1179 | pmid =  12582236| doi = 10.1093/NAR/GKG221 | pmc = 150239 | s2cid = 15125002}}</ref> and >45% GFP in tobacco leaves.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Yu Q, Tungsuchat-Huang T, Verma K, Radler MR, Maliga P | title =  Independent translation of ORFs in dicistronic operons, synthetic building blocks for polycistronic chloroplast gene expression | journal = Plant J. | date = August 1985 | volume = 103 | issue = 6 | pages = 2318–2329 | pmid =  32497322| doi = 10.1111/tpj.14864 | s2cid = 219328497| doi-access = free }}</ref> Their current goal is expression of orally bioavailable recombinant proteins in tobacco and lettuce chloroplasts.
